grammar.title: 4A: Obligation and prohibition - have to, must, should
grammar.explanation:
We use **have to** and **must** + infinitive to talk about obligation — something that is necessary to do.

**Have to** is for general or external rules. You **have to** send your resume before the deadline, and your colleague **has to** arrive before nine.

**Must** is for personal decisions or specific occasions. I **must** prepare for my interview tonight — that is my own decision, not a rule.

To say something is prohibited, use **mustn't**. You **mustn't** be late for your interview — it is not allowed.

**Don't have to** means there is no obligation. You **don't have to** work overtime if you finish before the deadline — it is your choice.

Use **should** / **shouldn't** + infinitive for advice or opinion, weaker than **must**. You **should** negotiate your salary before you sign the contract. **Ought to** is a more formal alternative.
examples: You *have to* send your resume before Friday. (company rule)
I *must* prepare for my interview tonight. (my own decision)
You *mustn't* use your phone during the interview. (prohibition)
We *don't have to* work overtime this week. (no obligation)
You *should* negotiate your salary before you accept the offer. (advice)

practice.q: Complete: A pilot ___ wear a uniform when he's at work. (rule, not a personal decision)
practice.a: has to — general/external rules take have to, not must.

practice.q: Complete: You ___ send text messages while you are driving. (it is prohibited)
practice.a: mustn't — mustn't means something is prohibited, not allowed.

practice.q: Complete: The museum is free, so we ___ pay. (no obligation)
practice.a: don't have to — don't have to means there is no obligation.
